"Mutually" is an adverb. It modifies a verb, adjective, or another adverb to express that something involves two (or more) parties equally — each toward the other, or both sharing the same thing.

The simplest way to think about it: "mutually" = "both toward each other" or "both together."

Imagine friendship. If you like someone but they don't like you back, that feeling is one-sided. But if you both like each other equally — the feeling flows in both directions — it is mutual. "Mutually" is the adverb that expresses this two-way quality.

1. Reciprocal — each does it to or for the other

Here, "mutually" says: whatever is happening, each party does it to the other. It's a back-and-forth.

  • "They mutually respect each other." → He respects her, and she respects him. Not one-sided.
  • "The countries mutually agreed to a ceasefire." → Each country agreed with the other. Neither was forced; both came to the agreement together.
  • "They mutually supported each other through hardship." → Each supported the other; the support was not one-directional.

2. Shared — both sides have or experience the same thing

Here, "mutually" says: something belongs to, applies to, or is felt by both parties equally. They "hold" it together.

  • "It was a mutually beneficial deal." → Good for both parties, not just one.
  • "The relationship was mutually satisfying." → Both people found it satisfying.
  • "A mutually held belief." → Both of them hold the same belief; it's common to both.

This is one of the most widely used applications of this word. "Mutually exclusive" means: two things that cannot both be true or exist at the same time. If one is true, the other is automatically ruled out.

Think of a coin flip. It can land either heads or tails — never both at once. Those are mutually exclusive outcomes.

More examples:

  • "Being in Delhi and Mumbai at the same time are mutually exclusive." → If you're in Delhi, you are automatically not in Mumbai.
  • "Sleeping and running are mutually exclusive activities." → You cannot do both simultaneously.
  • "Being honest and being kind are not always mutually exclusive." → This means they can coexist — you can be both at once.

The word "mutually" matters here because the exclusion works in both directions equally. It is not that A blocks B while B could still somehow exist independently — each one rules out the other, symmetrically.

This is a subtle but important distinction.

"Both sides benefit" simply states a fact: two parties each get something. "Mutually beneficial" says more — it implies the benefit arises from the relationship itself, that it is built into the arrangement, and that the two-way nature is the whole point.

Similarly, "they both agreed" just means two people happened to have the same opinion. "They mutually agreed" emphasizes that the agreement was reached together, through each other, as a shared act — not a coincidence.

"Mutually" highlights the connection between the parties, not just the fact that there are two of them.

• "The two firms mutually decided to end their partnership." → Both companies reached that decision together; it was not forced on one by the other.
  • "Their feelings were mutually understood." → Each understood the other's feelings; the understanding flowed in both directions.
  • "The terms were mutually acceptable." → Acceptable to both sides, not just one.
  • "The two events are mutually dependent." → Each one depends on the other; it is not a one-way dependency.
  • "Wealth and wisdom are not mutually exclusive." → A person can have both; one does not rule out the other.

It does not mean "separately." "They mutually decided" does not mean they each decided on their own in isolation — it means they decided together, through a shared process.

It does not mean "equally in amount." "Mutually beneficial" does not require both sides to gain exactly the same thing — just that both sides gain something.

It does not apply to one-sided situations. You would not say "she mutually loves him" if only she loves him and he does not love her back. The word only makes sense when both sides are genuinely involved.

"Mutually" = something shared between two or more parties, each toward the other, or held equally in common by both.

It signals a two-way relationship or shared condition. Use it when something does not just belong to or affect one side, but flows between all sides — whether they are doing something to each other, sharing the same experience, or both governed by the same rule or condition.
